description:
AGRO SENSE BOTS

I’m a developer passionate about technology and problem solving. I love turning ideas into working prototypes and finding creative solutions to real-world problems. Working with electronics, software, and AI has taught me that a good solution starts with the right question. I’m joining NASA Space Apps to explore space data and open science, meet people with new perspectives, and learn by building. AGRO SENSE BOTS: a team that starts with curiosity and grows by creating.
summary:
TradeSpace is a browser game that lets players feel the core of space mission design: every gain costs something. The player picks an Earth-observation, Moon or Mars mission, then chooses the orbit, launcher, instruments, and the power, communications and data systems. Mass, power and budget limits are computed live from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, launcher capacity and a cost model, and a Monte Carlo analysis shows launch and mission risk. When the design is done, a 3D flight plays out: each mission has its own rocket, spacecraft and route (Moon transfer, Mars Hohmann arc, ground track).
There are three modes: a story-driven Kids mode, a quick Mission Pilot mode and a full Professional mode with all parameters, risk and a report. In Mission Pilot mode, the Satellite Atlas shows real satellites such as the ISS, Hubble, GPS, GOES-19 and Chandra on their true orbits; clicking one opens a 3D model and its specifications. The game also includes a CubeSat 101-based development timeline and Go/No-Go review, a comparison with real NASA missions (MRO, MAVEN, Landsat 9, ICESat-2) and a 2-4 player team mode.
Data comes from NASA, ESA, NOAA and USGS sources; anything unverified is clearly labelled in the game. The goal is to let anyone feel the trade-offs engineers face every day.
details:
Trade Space is a browser-based game that teaches the trade-offs (mass, power, cost, data) in space mission design through gameplay. The player chooses an Earth observation, Moon, or Mars mission; determines the orbit, launch vehicle, satellite components, and scientific instruments. The game instantly calculates these choices using the rocket equation (Tsiolkovsky), launch vehicle capacity, power, communication, and data balance, and a cost model. Each mission's rocket, satellite, and trajectory are tracked in 3D during launch. A Monte Carlo analysis of 300 flights shows the risk; finally, a report explains why the mission succeeded or failed. There are three modes: a story mode for children, a fast-paced "Adventure" mode, and a full-parameter Professional mode. The Adventure mode includes a Satellite Atlas showing real satellites like the ISS, Hubble, GPS, GOES-19, and Chandra in their orbits.

Benefits:

No installation required, suitable for all ages, works in Turkish and English. Players learn through experience why a decision means compromising something. Can be used in education and STEM activities. The 2-4 person team mode is suitable for classroom use.

Intended impact

To make young and curious people feel the "every gain has a price" mentality of space engineering, and to increase interest in space missions.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (library-free game engine), Three.js for 3D rendering, Playwright for automated testing and screen recording, ffmpeg for video. No special hardware was required; the game runs in a browser, and switches to data mode if 3D rendering cannot be accessed. Data was sourced from NASA CubeSat 101, NASA mission press files, USGS, ESA, NOAA and Chandra X-ray Center; unverified values ​​are marked in the game. Artificial intelligence (Claude, Anthropic) was used in the game's interface and transitions.

Creativity

Instead of a single calculation screen, we made the trade-off the game itself. The same physics engine is explained differently to three different audiences (children, adventurers, professionals). Each mission has a different rocket, satellite and flight path; the Satellite Atlas shows real orbits live.

Factors considered:

Accuracy (sourced data, honest labeling), accessibility (no installation required, bilingual, different age groups), performance (backup mode if 3D cannot be opened), and educational value.
